source: Web research (WebSearch + WebFetch), Aug 2026. Primary sources fetched: docs.wpilib.org (tuning tutorials, SysId, feedforward, PID, bang-bang, picking-control-strategy, yearly changelogs for 2026 AND 2027), raw frc-docs RST on GitHub, github.wpilib.org Javadoc (ArmFeedforward, LinearSystemId, LinearQuadraticRegulator, ExponentialProfile, LTVUnicycleController, Matrix), CTRE Phoenix 6 docs (basic-pid-control, swerve-builder-api), REV REVLib docs (closed-loop, getting-started-with-pid-tuning), YAGSL docs (how-to-tune-pidf raw MD), YAMS gitbook (llms.txt, Live Tuning, elevator/arm tutorials, SmartMotorControllerConfig), DogLog docs (tunable-values), AdvantageScope docs (tuning mode), AdvantageKit docs (sysid-compatibility), GitHub raw source (6328 LoggedTunableNumber.java via hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt, hammerheads5000/TunableControls, hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt Drive.java), FrcCatalyst docs site, Prosper-FRC/utility-main-autoPIDTuner, FRC-Sonic-Squirrels/Flywheel-Tuner. Chief Delphi blocks WebFetch with HTTP 403; three CD threads were read via the r.jina.ai text proxy and are therefore SECOND-HAND summaries, flagged inline.
summary: WPILib's official pedagogy is now four browser-interactive tuning tutorials (flywheel/turret/vertical-arm/elevator) that teach a strict order of operations — gravity/static first (kG, kS), then kV, then kA, then kP, then kD, with an explicit "integral gain is generally not recommended for FRC" warning — and every tutorial ships concrete reference gains (turret kV=0.15/kP=0.3/kD=0.05; flywheel kV=0.0075/kP=0.1; arm kG=1.75/kV=1.95/kP=5/kD=1; elevator kG=2.28/kV=3.07/kA=0.41/kP=2.0). SysId 2026 is a four-command, off-robot round trip (bind quasistatic/dynamic fwd+rev → run → DataLogTool pull → drag the test-state entry into the Data Selector → read gains → retype → redeploy), and critically it still exposes an LQR-based Feedback Analysis that derives kP/kD from kV/kA plus max-acceptable-error / max-control-effort / measurement-delay — which is fully reimplementable ON the robot today with `LinearSystemId.identifyPositionSystem(kV,kA)` + `LinearQuadraticRegulator(plant,q,r,dt)` + `latencyCompensate()`, and the kS/kV/kA fit itself is a 3-4 column ordinary least squares that can be accumulated as O(1)-memory normal equations using bundled EJML / `Matrix.solveFullPivHouseholderQr`. The live-tuning ecosystem has converged on NT4 + AdvantageScope tuning mode: 6328's `LoggedTunableNumber` (key prefix `/Tuning`, `hasChanged(hashCode())` / static `ifChanged`), DogLog's `DogLog.tunable(key, default, consumer)` with automatic FMS gating, YAMS's `NT:/SmartDashboard/<MECH>/Commands/<SUBSYSTEM>/Live Tuning`, and FrcCatalyst's `/Catalyst/Tuning/<Mechanism>/{kP,kI,kD,kS,kV,kA,kG,MM/*}` with `tunableGains.checkAndApply(motor)` → `motor.updateSlot0(...)`. No FRC team has shipped a real auto-tuner: Prosper-FRC/utility-main-autoPIDTuner has a README but NO `src` directory (5 commits, stub), and the CD consensus (second-hand via proxy) is that relay/Åström–Hägglund autotune is inferior to hand tuning and "not for the uninitiated" — leaving a genuine, unoccupied niche for an on-robot guided tuner. The hard 2027 constraint dominates architecture: SystemCore replaces roboRIO, Java 25/C++23, NT3 removed, Shuffleboard + SmartDashboard + PathWeaver + RobotBuilder removed, `RamseteController`/`RamseteCommand` and `Mecanum`/`SwerveControllerCommand` removed, LTV controllers lose their LUTs, `Command.schedule()` deprecated, field coordinate origin changes, and Commands v3 + OpMode land alongside v2.
stack:
TARGET (2026, concluded season): WPILib 2026.2.1/2026.2.2 (Java 17), roboRIO 2. CTRE Phoenix 6 v26.1.x (firmware must match API year; Tuner X 2026 requires 2026 server). REVLib 2026 (Spark MAX/Flex, MAXMotion). AdvantageKit + AdvantageScope 2026 (Tuning Mode, `/Tuning` NT table). DogLog (jonahsnider/Team 581). Elastic 2026.1.2 (Gold872 — most-used driver dashboard). YAGSL (swerve) + YAMS (Yet Another Mechanism System, vendordep https://yet-another-software-suite.github.io/YAMS/yams.json, Java + C++, 400+ teams claimed). UPCOMING (2027, in alpha as of Aug 2026 — allwpilib 2027.0.0-alpha-6): SystemCore replaces roboRIO (multiple CAN buses, Smart IO, onboard IMU; removes relays, analog out, SPI). MotionCore. Unified FRC+FTC software experience. Java 25 / C++ 23. Ubuntu LTS only; Windows 10 support ending. NetworkTables v3 support REMOVED (NT4 only). New Driver Station app. Commands v3 (Java) + OpMode framework + declarative state-machine API on commands v3. REMOVED: Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver, RobotBuilder, `RamseteController`, `RamseteCommand`, `MecanumControllerCommand`, `SwerveControllerCommand`, LUTs inside LTV controllers. patterns.name: WPILib canonical tuning order-of-operations (per mechanism archetype)
patterns.whatItDoes: Four official browser-interactive tutorials, each teaching FF-first-then-FB with a fixed gain order and a reference answer. FLYWHEEL (velocity): tune kV alone until it reaches setpoint, back off on overshoot, then add kP → kV=0.0075, kP=0.1, kI=0, kD=0 for setpoint 300; D unnecessary for constant setpoints; pure-feedback is explicitly called poor because 'a non-zero amount of control effort is required' to hold velocity. TURRET (position, no gravity): pure feedback is acceptable; FF-only is bad because 'the feedforward equation relates velocity and acceleration to voltage' and cannot hold position (causes a 'kick' on setpoint change); kA unusable without motion profiling. Combined answer kV=0.15, kP=0.3, kD=0.05 (FF-only answer kV=0.2; FB-only answer kP=0.3, kD=0.05). VERTICAL ARM: set kG and kV to zero → raise kG until the arm holds position with as little movement as possible (docs say you must zero in on kG 'fairly precisely, at least four decimal places'; if it moves the other way, decrease) → raise kV until it tracks smooth slow motion → then kP, then kD. Answer kG=1.75, kV=1.95, kP=5, kD=1. kS and kA deliberately omitted from the tutorial. ELEVATOR: feedback-only is explicitly labeled 'not a good control scheme for vertical elevators!' (best-effort kP=10.0, kI=2.5, kD=0 still inconsistent across setpoints); the recommended path is motion-profiled FF+FB — start with conservative constraints 0.3 m/s and 0.3 m/s², tune kG to stop drift, kV to match the straight slopes of the profile, kA to match the curved (accel) segments, then kP as fine trim. Answer kG=2.28, kV=3.07, kA=0.41, kP=2.0.
patterns.libraryValue: This is THE spec for a guided tuner. Rootstock should encode these as a machine-readable state machine: `TuningRecipe.forFlywheel() / forTurret() / forArm() / forElevator()`, each a list of TuningSteps (gain under test, what the student should watch for, pass/fail criterion, next step). Because WPILib publishes reference answers, Rootstock can ship a self-check: run the recipe against WPILib's own sim classes (FlywheelSim/ElevatorSim/SingleJointedArmSim) and assert convergence near the documented gains. The 'kG to 4 decimal places' note is the single strongest argument for on-robot bisection instead of redeploy-and-guess.
patterns.codeSketch:
// Recipe as data, driven on-robot:
TuningRecipe.arm()
  .step("kG", Bisect.until(ArmHoldsStill), hint("arm drifts DOWN -> raise kG; drifts UP -> lower kG"))
  .step("kS", Ramp.untilBreakaway())
  .step("kV", Match.slope(profileVelocity))
  .step("kA", Match.curve(profileAccel))
  .step("kP", Exponential.until(Overshoot).thenBackOff(0.5))
  .step("kD", Exponential.until(Jitter).thenBackOff(0.5));

patterns.name: SysIdRoutine 2026 (the official, off-robot round trip)
patterns.whatItDoes: `new SysIdRoutine(Config, Mechanism)`. Config = (quasistatic ramp rate, default 1 V/s; dynamic step voltage, default 7 V; timeout, default 10 s; state callback, default null = log to WPILog). Mechanism = (voltage Consumer, log Consumer, Subsystem, optional name). Exposes `routine.quasistatic(Direction)` and `routine.dynamic(Direction)` as Commands — 4 tests total (quasi fwd/rev, dynamic fwd/rev). Fits per-mechanism models: simple `V = kS·sgn(ḋ) + kV·ḋ + kA·d̈`; elevator adds `+kG`; arm `V = kG·cos(θ) + kS·sgn(θ̇) + kV·θ̇ + kA·θ̈`. Analysis reports acceleration r², simulated-velocity r² (>0.9 = good fit), and simulated-velocity RMSE; accel r² below ~0.2 means dubious kA and rarely exceeds 0.5 even on good data. Workflow: run 4 tests → pull WPILog with DataLogTool → Log Loader → drag the string entry containing 'state' into Data Selector's Test State slot. Hard constraint: 'Only log files with a single routine in them are usable for analysis.' Drive ID needs 10–20 ft and cannot be done on blocks.
patterns.libraryValue: Rootstock should generate the whole routine from a mechanism config (as YAMS does — see below) so students never hand-write the two callbacks, and should own the log hygiene (one routine per file, auto-named, auto-timestamped). The 10 s / 7 V / 1 V·s⁻¹ defaults are unsafe for short-travel elevators and arms; a mechanism-aware library should derive ramp rate and step voltage from soft limits and measured travel instead of using constants.

patterns.name: LQR-derived kP/kD from kV/kA — SysId's Feedback Analysis, reproducible ON the robot
patterns.whatItDoes: SysId's Feedback Analysis view 'can be used to calculate optimal feedback gains for a PD or P controller for your mechanism (via LQR)'. Inputs: loop type (position or velocity), Max Acceptable Error, Max Acceptable Control Effort (docs: 'should never exceed 12V'), and measurement delay (auto-handled for stock smart-motor-controller filters; else d = T(n−1)/2 for sampling period T and window size n). 'Smaller values for Max Acceptable Error and larger values for Max Acceptable Control Effort will result in larger gains.' WPILib explicitly frames the output as 'educated guesses ... a starting point for further tuning'. Every piece is already in wpimath Java: `LinearSystemId.identifyPositionSystem(double kV, double kA)` → `LinearSystem<N2,N1,N2>` (states [pos, vel]); `LinearSystemId.identifyVelocitySystem(kV,kA)` → `LinearSystem<N1,N1,N1>`; `new LinearQuadraticRegulator(plant, qelms, relms, dtSeconds)` where qelms = 'maximum desired error tolerance for each state' and relms = 'maximum desired control effort for each input'; `lqr.latencyCompensate(plant, dtSeconds, inputDelaySeconds)`; `lqr.getK()`.
patterns.whereSeen: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/system-identification/analyzing-gains.html | https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/system/plant/LinearSystemId.html | https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/controller/LinearQuadraticRegulator.html (NOTE: I could not fetch sysid's FeedbackAnalysis.cpp itself — guessed raw paths 404'd — so the exact Q/R construction inside SysId is inferred from WPILib prose + the public wpimath API, not read from source)
patterns.libraryValue: This is the single highest-leverage feature for Rootstock and it needs zero new math. Once kV/kA exist (from SysId, from ReCalc, or from Rootstock's own on-robot fit), the library can hand a student kP/kD instantly with two physically meaningful sliders — 'how much error do you tolerate' and 'how many volts may I spend' — instead of an unitless kP they have to guess the magnitude of. It also removes the biggest SysId pain (the PC round trip) for the feedback half of the problem entirely.

patterns.name: On-robot ordinary-least-squares fit of kS/kV/kA/kG via streaming normal equations
patterns.whatItDoes: SysId's feedforward half is just OLS on an overdetermined system — WPILib describes it as a 'curve-fitting technique (such as least-squares regression)' over the mechanism model. The regressor rows are: simple → [sgn(v), v, a]; elevator → [1, sgn(v), v, a]; arm → [cos θ, sgn(v), v, a]. Because there are only 3–4 columns, you never need to store N samples: accumulate XᵀX (3×3 or 4×4) and Xᵀy (3×1 or 4×1) incrementally and solve once. wpimath ships everything needed: `Matrix.solve(b)` ('Returns the solution x to the equation Ax = b'; uses pseudo-inverse for non-square) and `Matrix.solveFullPivHouseholderQr(other)` ('Solves the least-squares problem Ax=B using a QR decomposition with full pivoting'). WPILib's Matrix is 'a shape-safe wrapper over Efficient Java Matrix Library (EJML)', and `org.ejml.simple.SimpleMatrix` is bundled and reachable if a runtime-sized matrix is ever needed.
patterns.libraryValue: Makes 'press a button, get kS/kV/kA/kG on the dashboard, no laptop' completely feasible on a roboRIO — the per-loop cost is a handful of multiply-adds and one 4×4 solve at the end. Combined with the LQR pattern above, Rootstock can close the entire loop on-robot: run profile → fit FF → derive PD → write to NT → optionally persist. Also report the same diagnostics SysId does (simulated-velocity r² > 0.9, accel r² > 0.2) so students learn to distrust bad fits rather than blindly accepting numbers.

patterns.name: LoggedTunableNumber (FRC 6328 Mechanical Advantage) — the de-facto standard tunable
patterns.whatItDoes: NT-backed double with a compile-time default, published under the fixed prefix `/Tuning`. Implements `DoubleSupplier`. `initDefault()` is idempotent (default can only be set once). Change detection is per-caller via a `Map<Integer,Double> lastHasChangedValues` keyed by an id — 'Recommended approach is to pass the result of hashCode()' — which is what lets multiple subsystems watch one tunable independently. Static `ifChanged(int id, Consumer<double[]> action, LoggedTunableNumber... nums)` fires once when ANY of a gain group changes and hands back all current values in declaration order; a `Runnable` overload exists too. Backed by AdvantageKit's `LoggedNetworkNumber`. Consumed by AdvantageScope: 'Any fields published to the /Tuning table on NetworkTables will appear under the Tuning table when using the NetworkTables 4 (AdvantageKit) live source', editable once tuning mode is toggled (slider icon right of the search bar; purple = active; numeric fields commit on blur or Enter).
patterns.libraryValue: Rootstock must be wire-compatible with `/Tuning` or students lose AdvantageScope tuning mode — that is a non-negotiable integration constraint, not a nice-to-have. But 6328's version has real gaps Rootstock should close: no AdvantageKit-free fallback (small teams often don't run AK), no min/max/step metadata, no units, no FMS gating, and no way to get the tuned value back into source. A `RootstockTunable` that publishes to `/Tuning`, degrades to plain NT4 without AdvantageKit, carries unit + range metadata, auto-ignores NT when `DriverStation.isFMSAttached()`, and can dump a paste-ready `Constants.java` snippet would be a strict superset.

patterns.name: Tunable controller WRAPPERS (hammerheads5000/TunableControls) — gains as a first-class object
patterns.whatItDoes: Third-party library that wraps WPILib controllers so gains self-update. Classes: `ControlConstants` (fluent builder holding kP/kI/kD, kS/kG/kV/kA, profile constraints, tolerance; factory methods `getPIDController()`, `getElevatorFeedforward()`), `TunableControlConstants` (same fields but each backed by a LoggedTunableNumber), `TunablePIDController`, `TunableProfiledController` (ProfiledPIDController + trapezoid profile + FF, with `calculateFeedforward()` and continuous-input support). README explicitly cites the motivation: avoiding 'issues that arise when multiple controller instances share the same name.' Distributed by copy-paste of TunableControls.java + LoggedTunableNumber.java — 'not yet available as a vendordep'; requires AdvantageKit. Publishes to the 'Tuning' NetworkTable for real-time adjustment in AdvantageScope.
patterns.libraryValue: Validates the core Rootstock abstraction: students should configure ONE `Gains` object per mechanism, and tunability, logging, profile constraints, tolerance and the FF/FB split should all fall out of it — not be wired by hand at each call site. The fact that this exists as copy-paste-only, AdvantageKit-required code is exactly the gap a small-team-focused vendordep fills. Steal the fluent `.withPID().withTolerance().withFeedforward().withProfile()` shape and the named-namespace fix.

patterns.name: DogLog tunable values — the AdvantageKit-free tunable, with FMS gating built in
patterns.whatItDoes: `DogLog.tunable(key, defaultValue)` returns a `DoubleSubscriber`; overloads accept a callback (`DogLog.tunable("Intake/Voltage", 4, v -> motor.setVoltage(v))`) and an optional unit as String / `Unit` / `Measure` so AdvantageScope renders it properly. Supports strings, numbers, booleans. Published to `Tunable/<key>` on NT and continuously mirrored into the `Robot/Tunable/` table of the DataLog with unit metadata. Crucially: 'By default, DogLog will ignore tunable values from NetworkTables when connected to the FMS on a competition field' — configurable via the `ntTunables` option in `DogLogOptions`.
patterns.libraryValue: Two ideas to copy outright. (1) The callback form removes the entire `hasChanged(hashCode())` boilerplate — the tunable pushes to the motor controller itself, so a student writing an elevator never types a change-detection `if`. (2) FMS auto-gating is a safety default every tunable system should have and 6328's does not; Rootstock should make it the default and require an explicit opt-out. Also note the unit metadata: shipping units on gains is what lets a dashboard show 'V·s/rad' next to kV instead of a bare number.

patterns.name: YAMS Live Tuning + one-line SysId — the closest existing competitor to Rootstock
patterns.whatItDoes: YAMS (Yet Another Mechanism System, vendordep, Java + C++) covers Arms, Elevators, Pivots (turrets/hoods), FlyWheels, SwerveDrives. Live Tuning activates when any tunable setpoint uses `TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH` and publishes to `NT:/SmartDashboard/<MECHANISM_NAME>/Commands/<SUBSYSTEM_NAME>/Live Tuning`, editable from AdvantageScope or Elastic. Exposes PID gains (kP in V/rot, kI in V/(rot·s), kD in V/(rot/s)), all three feedforward flavors (SimpleMotorFeedforward kS/kV/kA; ArmFeedforward kS/kG/kV/kA; ElevatorFeedforward kS/kG/kV/kA), trapezoidal AND exponential profile constraints, soft limits, stator/supply current limits, voltage compensation and ramp rates. All values published in SI-adjacent units (rot, rot/s, m, m/s, V, A, °C). Doc carries an explicit warning: 'Live Tuning can be DANGEROUS please test in sim before the real' robot. SysId is a ONE-LINER on the mechanism. Config is a deep fluent builder with separate real/sim gains (`withClosedLoopController` vs `withSimClosedLoopController`, `withFeedforward` vs `withSimFeedforward`), `withExponentialProfile(Voltage, DCMotor, Mass, Distance)` etc., `withClosedLoopController(LQRController)`, and gearing as `GearBox.fromReductionStages(3,4)`. Also integrates Phoenix Tuner X with YAMS physics sim through a vendorsim layer so TalonFX/TalonFXS signals update live in Tuner X.
patterns.libraryValue: This is the bar Rootstock must clear, and it is high. Differentiators still available: YAMS's Live Tuning is a manual slider panel — it tells you WHERE the knobs are, not WHICH ONE TO TURN NEXT. Nothing in YAMS runs the WPILib recipe for you, bisects kG, derives kP/kD from kV/kA via LQR, scores the fit, or teaches. Also note YAMS's NT path lives under `/SmartDashboard/...` (SmartDashboard is REMOVED in 2027) while 6328/AdvantageScope use `/Tuning` — Rootstock should pick `/Tuning`. Steal outright: separate sim vs real gains in config (lets a student tune in sim first, which the danger warning demands), and the one-line `sysId(...)` command factory.
patterns.codeSketch:
// One-line SysId, mechanism-aware:
public Command sysId() { return elevator.sysId(Volts.of(7), Volts.of(2).per(Second), Seconds.of(4)); }

new SmartMotorControllerConfig(this)
  .withControlMode(ControlMode.CLOSED_LOOP)
  .withDrumRadius(Inches.of(0.25), 22)
  .withClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0)
  .withTrapezoidalProfile(MetersPerSecond.of(0.5), MetersPerSecondPerSecond.of(0.5))
  .withSimClosedLoopController(4, 0, 0)
  .withFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0, 0, 0))
  .withSimFeedforward(new ElevatorFeedforward(0, 0, 0))
  .withTelemetry("ElevatorMotor", TelemetryVerbosity.HIGH)
  .withGearing(new MechanismGearing(GearBox.fromReductionStages(3, 4)))
  .withStatorCurrentLimit(Amps.of(40));

patterns.name: FrcCatalyst TunableGains.checkAndApply() — push tuned gains straight into vendor Slot0Configs
patterns.whatItDoes: 2026 Phoenix-6-oriented mechanism library. Gains published under `/Catalyst/Tuning/<MechanismName>/` as `kP, kI, kD, kS, kV, kA, kG` plus `MM/CruiseVelocity`, `MM/Acceleration`, `MM/Jerk`. A `TunableGains` helper is polled every periodic — 'On every periodic, the mechanism calls tunableGains.checkAndApply(motor)' — which detects per-gain changes and calls `motor.updateSlot0(kP,kI,kD,kS,kV,kA,kG)` and `motor.updateMotionMagic(...)`; the gravity model persists across re-applies. Tuning is ON by default; `TunableNumber.disableTuning()` in `robotInit()` during a match makes every `get()` return its cached default in constant time. Live tuning is supported for LinearMechanism, RotationalMechanism, FlywheelMechanism (PID/FF only), DifferentialWristMechanism. SysId quasistatic/dynamic routines are built into every mechanism. Also ships MotionConstraintCalculator (physics-derived velocity/accel limits) and StateSpaceController (LQR + Kalman).
patterns.whereSeen: https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/ | https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning (NOTE: read from the project's own docs site only; I did not read its source, so implementation claims are the authors')
patterns.libraryValue: The `checkAndApply(motor)` shape is the right ergonomic for on-controller closed loops (Phoenix 6 / REV), which is where most small teams actually run their loops — the tunable must write THROUGH to Slot0Configs, not just sit in an NT table next to a roboRIO-side PIDController. Note the design tension worth resolving explicitly in Rootstock: `checkAndApply` every periodic risks CAN config spam, so gate on change detection and rate-limit. The constant-time disabled path is also the right answer for match-time overhead.

patterns.name: 2026 feedforward API: discrete plant-inversion via calculateWithVelocities (the old calculate() is deprecated for removal)
patterns.whatItDoes: `ArmFeedforward` 2026 constructors: `(ks,kg,kv)`, `(ks,kg,kv,ka)`, `(ks,kg,kv,ka,dtSeconds)`. Live calculate methods: `calculate(double positionRadians, double velocity)` and `calculateWithVelocities(double currentAngle, double currentVelocity, double nextVelocity)`. BOTH `calculate(pos, vel, accel)` and `calculate(currentAngle, currentVelocity, nextVelocity, dt)` are `@Deprecated(forRemoval=true, since="2025")`. Mutable gains via `setKs/setKg/setKv/setKa` + `getKs/getKg/getKv/getKa/getDt` — i.e. WPILib itself now supports live-retuning a feedforward in place. Also `maxAchievableVelocity(maxVoltage, angle, acceleration)`, `minAchievableVelocity(...)`, `maxAchievableAcceleration(maxVoltage, angle, velocity)`, `minAchievableAcceleration(...)`. Gain units: SimpleMotorFeedforward kS=V, kV=V·s/distance, kA=V·s²/distance; ArmFeedforward kS=V, kG=V, kV=V·s/rad, kA=V·s²/rad; ElevatorFeedforward kS=V, kG=V, kV=V·s/distance, kA=V·s²/distance. 2027 changelog: 'Clean up arm and elevator feedforward APIs' and 'Fix SimpleMotorFeedforward no-accel overload returning negative voltage outputs'.
patterns.libraryValue: Rootstock must default to `calculateWithVelocities(pos, currentVel, nextVel)` fed from consecutive profile setpoints — the accel-based overload will be deleted, and teaching students the deprecated call would age the library out in one season. The existing setKs/setKg/setKv/setKa setters mean Rootstock's live retune does NOT need to reallocate feedforward objects on every gain change. The maxAchievable*/minAchievable* helpers are underused and are exactly the right way to auto-derive safe motion-profile constraints from measured gains instead of asking a student to guess m/s².

patterns.name: Swerve tuning: published starting gains, and drive-as-flywheel / steer-as-turret framing
patterns.whatItDoes: YAGSL's pedagogy: 'The drive motor should be tuned as if it were a flywheel' (→ use the WPILib flywheel tutorial) and the steer/angle motor as a position controller (→ turret tutorial); steer has continuous input wrapping enabled at the top and bottom, so 'when tuning your PID you may want to test with left or right translation' rather than rotation. Published starting points — SparkMax: drive p=0.0020645, angle p=0.01 (i=d=f=iz=0). TalonFX/Kraken/Falcon: drive p=1, angle p=50, d=0.32. CTRE Tuner X Swerve Project Generator emits `steerGains = new Slot0Configs().withKP(100).withKI(0).withKD(0.5).withKS(0.1).withKV(1.91).withKA(0).withStaticFeedforwardSign(StaticFeedforwardSignValue.UseClosedLoopSign)` and `driveGains = new Slot0Configs().withKP(0.1).withKI(0).withKD(0).withKS(0).withKV(0.124)`, with the doc noting 'Both sets of gains need to be tuned to your individual robot' and that 'drive kS and kV gains should always be characterized'. SECOND-HAND (r.jina.ai proxy of CD): in the 'Tuning CTRE Swerve' thread, poster nexnot says kP is 'realistically the most important by far', tune it until it JUST starts oscillating, and 'don't even bother with kI or kD'; the same thread's root cause for chronic oscillation was 'applying the same motor configs to both our drive and turn motors'. Also second-hand: with TorqueCurrentFOC, kV is negligible on swerve drive motors so only kS and kP remain.
patterns.libraryValue: Two concrete features. (1) Ship vendor-and-mechanism-keyed DEFAULT gains so a student's first deploy moves sanely instead of doing nothing or exploding — the 0.0020645-vs-1.0 and 0.01-vs-50 spreads show that a single 'kP = 1' default is actively harmful and that the library must know which vendor's units it's in. (2) Reuse: Rootstock should literally implement swerve drive tuning by delegating to its flywheel recipe and steer tuning to its turret recipe, which is both correct and a great teaching story. Also worth a guardrail: warn when identical configs are applied to drive and steer motors, and warn when continuous wrapping is on but the student is testing with rotation.

patterns.name: Flywheel/shooter: BangBangController + 0.9× feedforward
patterns.whatItDoes: `edu.wpi.first.math.controller.BangBangController`. 'When controlling the velocity of high-inertia mechanisms under varying loads (like a shooter flywheel), a bang-bang controller can yield faster recovery time and thus better/more consistent performance than a proportional controller.' Two hard warnings: motor controllers MUST be in coast mode ('or else the braking action will fight the controller and cause potentially destructive oscillation') and 'it is a very bad idea to use a bang-bang controller on anything other than velocity control of a high-inertia mechanism.' Canonical usage multiplies the controller output by 12.0 V and adds 0.9× the feedforward — the 0.9 deliberately under-shoots 'to avoid overspeeding the shooter' since bang-bang can only correct upward. Separately, the flywheel tutorial notes plain bang-bang has no tunable parameters at all and oscillates from loop delay.
patterns.libraryValue: A `RootstockFlywheel` should offer bang-bang+0.9·FF as a named, one-flag strategy AND refuse to enable it unless idle mode is coast — that safety interlock is a library's job, not a student's memory. It's also the best 'you barely have to tune anything' answer for a small team with a shooter, which is squarely the target user.

patterns.name: Teaching: WPILib's in-browser sims, the P/I/D one-liner, and the spring/damper analogies
patterns.whatItDoes: WPILib's four tuning tutorials embed live JavaScript simulations directly in the docs — raw HTML divs with a per-sim class instantiated on load (`new FlywheelBangBang("flywheel_bb")`, `FlywheelPIDF` taking a mode of 'feedforward' | 'feedback' | 'both'), laid out as `{prefix}_plotVals` (velocity plot), `{prefix}_plotVolts` (voltage plot), `{prefix}_viz` (mechanism cartoon), `{prefix}_ctrls` (gain inputs). The elevator sim lets you 'change the elevator setpoint by clicking on the desired height'; noise can be toggled on after you've mastered the ideal case; the tutorials teach exponential/orders-of-magnitude search for gains. WPILib's own analogies: proportional gain acts like 'software-defined springs that pull the system toward the desired position'; derivative acts like damping / a door closer, 'tries to make the output move at the same rate as the reference'. Blunt warning: 'Integral gain is generally not recommended for FRC use. It is almost always better to use a feedforward controller to eliminate steady-state error. If you do employ integral gain, it is crucial to provide some protection against integral windup.' The community's most-repeated one-liner (YAGSL, sourced to a CD thread + YouTube video): 'P: if you're not where you want to be, get there. I: if you haven't been where you want to be for a long time, get there faster. D: if you're getting close to where you want to be, slow down.'
patterns.whereSeen: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tutorial-intro.html | https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/introduction-to-pid.html | https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wpilibsuite/frc-docs/main/source/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-flywheel.rst (raw HTML + JS embed pattern) | https://docs.yagsl.com/configuring-yagsl/how-to-tune-pidf | https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/finally-i-understand-pid/450811 | https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qKy98Cbcltw | non-FRC interactive demos: https://github.com/ANRGUSC/pid-drone-control , https://eliottwiener.github.io/pidcontroldemo/ , https://tools.softinery.com/PIDSIM/
patterns.libraryValue: Don't build a new PID explainer — build the bridge from WPILib's sim to the student's actual robot. Highest-value teaching feature: make Rootstock's tuning UI show the SAME two stacked plots as the docs (measured-vs-setpoint on top, commanded volts below) so the shape a student learned in the browser is literally the shape they see on their elevator. Second: because WPILib's tutorials publish reference gains, Rootstock can ship 'practice mode' — run the recipe against WPILib's ElevatorSim/SingleJointedArmSim/FlywheelSim with the docs' plant and let a student tune a virtual mechanism, with noise toggleable, before touching hardware (which also satisfies YAMS's 'test in sim before the real robot' warning). Third: adopt WPILib's exact vocabulary (springs, damping) and its anti-I stance, and have the library actively discourage kI — e.g. require an explicit `.withIntegral(kI, iZone, maxIntegral)` that forces the student to supply windup protection.

patterns.name: Dashboard write-back surface: what a tunable can actually be edited from in 2026
patterns.whatItDoes: Elastic (most-used FRC driver dashboard) editable widgets — Text Display (boolean/float/double/int and arrays) YES, Number Slider (double) YES, Toggle Button YES, Toggle Switch YES, ComboBox/Split Button Chooser YES, Command YES, RobotPreferences YES, PIDController sendable YES, DifferentialDrive YES, Relay YES. NOT editable: Large Text Display, Number Bar, Voltage View, Radial Gauge, Graph, Boolean Box, color views, Encoder, Gyro, Field, SwerveDrive, Subsystem, Alerts. AdvantageScope: read-only by default; toggle tuning mode via the slider icon right of the search bar (purple = on), numeric fields commit on blur or Enter, booleans toggle by clicking the red/green circle; AdvantageKit-published fields are output-only, but user-published `/Tuning` fields are editable. WPILib `Preferences` persists to roboRIO flash for 'calibration settings for potentiometers, PID values, setpoints ... that you would like to change without having to rebuild the program'. Sendable-based tuning uses `addDoubleProperty(name, getter, setter)`; `PIDController` is already Sendable. SECOND-HAND (proxy of CD 'How are teams implementing adjustable constants', thread 507361): teams report SmartDashboard causing loop-time overruns and prefer writing NT directly via Elastic/AdvantageScope; Sendables were called the most accessible path requiring no architectural change; DogLog TunablePID and YAMS `NT:/Tuning` were both cited.
patterns.libraryValue: Determines Rootstock's wire format. Publish plain NT4 doubles under `/Tuning/<Mechanism>/<gain>` so BOTH Elastic (Text Display / Number Slider) and AdvantageScope tuning mode work with zero extra setup, and never depend on SmartDashboard/Shuffleboard (both deleted in 2027). Ship a prebuilt Elastic layout JSON per mechanism archetype so a student gets a working tuning tab without dragging widgets. Offer `Preferences` as an optional persistence backend so tuned gains survive a reboot without a redeploy — that closes the 'we tuned it, then power-cycled, and lost everything' failure. Do NOT rely on the PIDController Sendable alone: it exposes kP/kI/kD but not kS/kV/kA/kG, which is where the real work is.

patterns.name: Vendor on-controller feedforward is now first-class — gains must be pushed, not just displayed
patterns.whatItDoes: PHOENIX 6: `Slot0Configs` carries kP/kI/kD/kS/kV/kA/kG plus GravityType and StaticFeedforwardSign. Semantics are output-relative, so units depend on the control request type (voltage vs duty cycle vs TorqueCurrentFOC). Position loop: kP = output/rotation, kI = output/(rotation·s), kD = output/rps, kS = output (static friction), kG = output (gravity); kV/kA unused. Velocity loop: kP = output/rps, kI = output/rotation, kD = output/(rps/s), kV = output/rps; kA only enters with a motion profile. Guidance: with a position loop at zero velocity reference, 'use the minimal amount of kS to avoid motor output dithering when closed loop error is near zero.' REVLIB 2026: onboard feedforward now supports kS, kV, kA, kG ('linear gravity feedforward, for an elevator'), kCos ('cosine gravity feedforward, for an arm') and kCosRatio ('relates the encoder position to absolute position') — kV formerly called kF. Units: position = rotations, velocity = RPM, MAXMotion cruise = RPM, accel = RPM/s; so kV is V/RPM, kA is V/(RPM/s), kS is V. REV recommends kP = 0.01 as a MAXMotion Position starting point in default units and states 'you should be able to get decent performance with only kV/kA and no PID at all.' REV's procedure: zero everything → verify safe to actuate → check/fix motor direction → 'Setup and tune any relevant feedforwards' → P very small relative to your units → increase until motion → increase to target speed → on oscillation reduce P or add a little D; 'Most teams find success using controllers tuned primarily with P and D, using a Feedforward to account for steady-state error'; use FF not I for steady-state error, and limit I to prevent windup if used.
patterns.libraryValue: Confirms the write-through requirement (FrcCatalyst pattern) and, more importantly, exposes the #1 conceptual trap Rootstock should abolish: kP means something completely different on a Talon (output per rotation, output = duty cycle OR volts OR amps depending on request), on a Spark (duty cycle per rotation, velocity in RPM), and in wpimath (volts per meter or per radian). Rootstock should define ALL gains in one canonical unit system — volts per SI unit, matching wpimath and WPILib's units library — and convert on the way into Slot0Configs/ClosedLoopConfig. Then the number a student learns from the WPILib arm tutorial transfers unchanged to their Kraken or their NEO, and the vendor-specific magic numbers stop being something a 15-year-old has to memorize. Note also that REV's kCos/kCosRatio means an arm's gravity FF can now run at 1 kHz on the controller rather than 50 Hz on the RIO — worth supporting.

patterns.name: Motion profiling + ProfiledPIDController + ExponentialProfile
patterns.whatItDoes: `ProfiledPIDController(kP, kI, kD, TrapezoidProfile.Constraints)` pairs trapezoidal setpoint generation with PID tracking; the standard combination adds feedforward computed from the profile's setpoint velocity. `ExponentialProfile` (nested `Constraints`, `State`, `ProfileTiming`): `calculate(double t, State current, State goal)`, `timeLeftUntil(current, goal)`, `calculateInflectionPoint(current, goal)` — 'the point after which the fastest way to reach the goal state is to apply input in the opposite direction' — and `calculateProfileTiming(current, goal)`. Constraints are built from characterization via `ExponentialProfile.Constraints.fromCharacteristics(maxInput, kV, kA)`, i.e. an exponential profile is derived directly from the SAME kV/kA SysId produces, unlike a trapezoid whose constraints are guessed. YAMS exposes it as `withExponentialProfile(Voltage, DCMotor, Mass, Distance)` / `(Voltage, DCMotor, MomentOfInertia)`. 2027: `TrapezoidProfile.State` and `ExponentialProfile.State` gain structs / StructSerializable, and a real bug fix landed — 'Fix TrapezoidProfile limiting velocity incorrectly'.
patterns.libraryValue: `fromCharacteristics(maxInput, kV, kA)` is the killer detail: once Rootstock has kV/kA it can hand a student a motion profile with ZERO additional tuning, which removes the two most arbitrary numbers in the whole workflow (max velocity and max acceleration, which students routinely set to physically impossible values). Recommend defaulting positional mechanisms to ExponentialProfile-from-characteristics and treating trapezoid as the opt-out. Pair with `maxAchievableVelocity/Acceleration` from the feedforward classes as a sanity check, and make profile setpoints the source for `calculateWithVelocities`.

painPoints.problem: Manual tuning consumes a full build day per subsystem, and beginners have no idea what magnitude to start at because kP/kI/kD are unitless to them
painPoints.evidence: CD 'PID Tuning Tips & Tricks' (read via r.jina.ai proxy, SECOND-HAND): teams report it takes programmers 'at least a day or more to dial in one subsystem'; poster LHACK4142 describes starting kP at 0.00001 and increasing by ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE until movement appears, then incrementing to slight overshoot and backing off, estimating 'maximum of 12 deploys to tune' — and notes kP/kI/kD have units (e.g. duty cycle per radian) that must be reasoned about. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pid-tuning-tips-tricks/502784 . The magnitude problem is real and vendor-dependent: YAGSL's own starting kP for the same swerve steer role is 0.01 (SparkMax) vs 50 (TalonFX) — a 5000x spread. https://docs.yagsl.com/configuring-yagsl/how-to-tune-pidf
painPoints.libraryFix: (a) Ship vendor-and-archetype-keyed default gains so the first deploy always does something visible and safe. (b) Replace the human 12-deploy exponential search with an on-robot automated exponential search + backoff that never requires a redeploy. (c) Define all gains in volts-per-SI-unit and convert at the vendor boundary, so kP has a physical meaning a student can reason about and transfers between a NEO and a Kraken. (d) Derive kP/kD from kV/kA via LQR with 'max error' and 'max volts' sliders, so the student's knobs are physical quantities rather than abstract gains.

painPoints.problem: The SysId round trip is a 9-step, laptop-bound ritual that a small team will do once, badly, and then never repeat
painPoints.evidence: Full 2026 workflow: write voltageDrive + logMotors callbacks → build SysIdRoutine → bind 4 commands → run quasistatic fwd, quasistatic rev, dynamic fwd, dynamic rev → pull the WPILog off the roboRIO with DataLogTool → open SysId Log Loader → drag the string entry containing 'state' into the Data Selector's Test State slot → read gains → retype into Constants.java → redeploy. Plus hard constraints: 'Only log files with a single routine in them are usable for analysis' (running sequential routines without extraction or power-cycling causes analysis failure), drive ID needs '10' of space, ideally closer to 20'', and 'the robot drive can not be accurately characterized while on blocks'. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/system-identification/creating-routine.html , .../running-routine.html , .../loading-data.html . AdvantageKit users hit an extra step: 'AdvantageKit log files should NOT be used directly with SysId' — you must re-export via AdvantageScope v3.0.2+ with WPILOG format and 'AdvantageKit Cycles' timestamps, because AK only records field CHANGES while SysId expects a sample every tick. https://docs.advantagekit.org/data-flow/sysid-compatibility/
painPoints.libraryFix: Do the fit on the robot. Accumulate XᵀX/Xᵀy during the same four sweeps and solve a 3×3 or 4×4 system at the end (Matrix.solveFullPivHouseholderQr), publishing kS/kV/kA/kG straight to /Tuning with the same quality metrics SysId reports (simulated-velocity r² > 0.9, accel r² > 0.2). Auto-manage log hygiene (one routine per file, auto-named). Auto-derive ramp rate and step voltage from the mechanism's soft limits and measured travel instead of the unsafe 1 V/s and 7 V defaults. Keep WPILog export as an escape hatch for teams that want the official tool, but never require it.

painPoints.problem: kG for an arm/elevator must be tuned far more precisely than a redeploy loop can support
painPoints.evidence: WPILib vertical-arm tutorial: increase kG until the arm holds position 'with as little movement as possible', and 'you will have to zero in on Kg fairly precisely, at least four decimal places'; if the arm moves the opposite way, decrease it. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/tuning-vertical-arm.html
painPoints.libraryFix: A dedicated on-robot `findKg()` routine: hold the mechanism near a known angle, binary-search the holding voltage against a measured-drift-rate objective, converge to 4+ decimals in seconds, and publish the result. This is the clearest single demonstration that on-robot beats redeploy-and-guess, and it is trivially safe (small voltages, bounded travel) — an ideal first feature.

painPoints.problem: Tuned values are stranded on the dashboard: there is no supported path from a good NT value back into source, and a power cycle loses everything
painPoints.evidence: 6328's LoggedTunableNumber reads from the dashboard and falls back to a compile-time default; nothing writes back. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt/main/src/main/java/frc/robot/util/LoggedTunableNumber.java . WPILib Preferences exists precisely to store 'PID values, setpoints, etc. that you would like to change without having to rebuild the program' in roboRIO flash, but it is a separate, manually-wired system with its own keys. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/basic-programming/robot-preferences.html . DogLog mirrors tunables into the DataLog but that is for post-hoc analysis, not code generation. https://doglog.dev/reference/tunable-values
painPoints.libraryFix: Two-part: (1) optional Preferences-backed persistence so tuned gains survive reboot without a redeploy; (2) a 'commit' command that emits a paste-ready Java constants block (or writes a JSON/TOML gains file the library loads at boot) to the console and to NT, so the student's afternoon of tuning becomes a reviewable diff instead of a screenshot. This is a genuinely unoccupied gap — no library found does it.

painPoints.problem: Tunable naming collides when the same controller class is instantiated multiple times, and the ecosystem has NOT converged on one NT path
painPoints.evidence: TunableControls README states its explicit motivation is avoiding 'issues that arise when multiple controller instances share the same name'. https://github.com/hammerheads5000/TunableControls . Competing paths in the wild: 6328/AdvantageScope use `/Tuning` (https://docs.advantagescope.org/overview/live-sources/tuning-mode/); DogLog uses `Tunable/<key>` on NT and `Robot/Tunable/` in the log (https://doglog.dev/reference/tunable-values); YAMS uses `NT:/SmartDashboard/<MECHANISM>/Commands/<SUBSYSTEM>/Live Tuning` (https://yagsl.gitbook.io/yams/documentation/understanding/integrations.md); FrcCatalyst uses `/Catalyst/Tuning/<Mechanism>/` (https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning). YAMS's choice is actively at risk — SmartDashboard is REMOVED in 2027 (https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html).
painPoints.libraryFix: Namespace every tunable as `/Tuning/<MechanismName>/<gain>` with the mechanism name required at construction (not defaulted), so collisions are structurally impossible and AdvantageScope tuning mode works out of the box. Publish plain NT4 doubles with no AdvantageKit dependency, and never route through SmartDashboard/Shuffleboard. Ship a duplicate-key detector that raises a WPILib Alert at construction rather than silently aliasing two mechanisms onto one slider.

painPoints.problem: Live tuning is genuinely dangerous and most implementations ship it enabled with no interlocks
painPoints.evidence: YAMS docs carry an explicit warning: 'Live Tuning can be DANGEROUS please test in sim before the real' robot. https://yagsl.gitbook.io/yams/documentation/understanding/integrations.md . SysId docs: 'Watch out for your mechanism and stop the test early if it exceeds safe limits! The routine only creates voltage commands for you to connect to your motors, it is up to you to set up hard or soft limits to prevent injury or damage.' https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/system-identification/running-routine.html . BangBangController: coast mode is mandatory 'or else the braking action will fight the controller and cause potentially destructive oscillation.' https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/bang-bang.html . REV's procedure warns 'This process will spin the motor, potentially at unexpected speeds and in unexpected directions.' https://docs.revrobotics.com/revlib/spark/closed-loop/getting-started-with-pid-tuning . FrcCatalyst ships tuning ENABLED by default. https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning
painPoints.libraryFix: Make safety structural, not documentary: require soft limits before any tuning routine will arm; clamp commanded volts to a configured ceiling; require a held enable button (whileTrue) so releasing the trigger stops the sweep; auto-abort on soft-limit approach, on stator current spike, or on velocity exceeding a derived ceiling; refuse bang-bang unless idle mode is coast; and default to running the whole recipe against the WPILib sim plant first, promoting to hardware only on explicit confirmation. This is the strongest possible differentiator for a SMALL-team library where no mentor is watching.

painPoints.problem: No shipped FRC auto-tuner exists — the one that advertises itself is an empty repository
painPoints.evidence: Prosper-FRC/utility-main-autoPIDTuner presents a full README (features/installation/usage) but the repo contains only .github/workflows, .run, gradle/wrapper, lib, vendordeps, README.md, gradle.properties, gradlew, gradlew.bat, settings.gradle — NO src directory, 5 commits total. The README names no algorithm, no classes, and no API. https://github.com/Prosper-FRC/utility-main-autoPIDTuner . FRC-Sonic-Squirrels/Flywheel-Tuner is real but is a manual single-purpose roboRIO app for NEO/Falcon flywheels (dashboard fields for CAN IDs and kF/kP/kI/kD, Xbox preset-RPM buttons), not an auto-tuner. https://github.com/FRC-Sonic-Squirrels/Flywheel-Tuner . CD 'Automatic PID Tuning' (proxy, SECOND-HAND): SLAB-Mr.Thomas ported an Arduino AutoTune library to FRC motors and reports it completes in ~0.25 s, but states hand tuning is 'usually rated as superior to the autotune relay method' and that auto-tune 'is not for the uninitiated'; Gerthworm redirected the thread to WPILib SysId as the proper answer. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/automatic-pid-tuning/426844 , https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/auto-tuning-pid/395040
painPoints.libraryFix: The niche is open — but ship GUIDED tuning, not blind autotuning, because the community's stated objection is pedagogical (auto-tune hides understanding), not technical. Concretely: (1) on-robot OLS for kS/kV/kA/kG; (2) LQR-derived kP/kD from kV/kA with physical sliders; (3) a step-by-step recipe runner that narrates WHY each step happens and shows the WPILib-style plots at every step; (4) automated bisection only for the objectively mechanical steps (kG hold, kS breakaway). Explicitly skip relay/Åström–Hägglund and Ziegler-Nichols: Z-N deliberately drives the loop to sustained oscillation, which is unsafe on a geared FRC arm or elevator, and the FRC-specific literature already says the results are worse than hand tuning. Say this out loud in the docs — it will preempt the exact objection the CD threads raise.

painPoints.problem: Students are taught to reach for kI, which WPILib says is almost always the wrong answer
painPoints.evidence: WPILib: 'Integral gain is generally not recommended for FRC use. It is almost always better to use a feedforward controller to eliminate steady-state error. If you do employ integral gain, it is crucial to provide some protection against integral windup.' https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/introduction/introduction-to-pid.html . REV echoes it: use feedforward for steady-state error, and if I is used it must be 'limited to prevent I windup'. https://docs.revrobotics.com/revlib/spark/closed-loop/getting-started-with-pid-tuning . Yet the canonical community mnemonic YAGSL republishes teaches I as a co-equal term ('if you haven't been where you want to be for a long time, get there faster'), and WPILib's own flywheel tutorial still walks students through adding kI when 'the output gets stuck'. https://docs.yagsl.com/configuring-yagsl/how-to-tune-pidf
painPoints.libraryFix: Make the correct path the easy one: no bare `.withI(kI)`. Require `.withIntegral(kI, iZone, maxIntegralVolts)` so windup protection is unskippable, and have the tuning recipe reach for kS/kG BEFORE ever offering I, with an inline explanation that steady-state error means a missing feedforward term. Emit a WPILib Alert when kI != 0 and kS == 0 on a mechanism archetype that should have one.

painPoints.problem: Mechanical slop and backlash defeat any amount of tuning, and nothing warns the student
painPoints.evidence: CD 'PID Tuning Tips & Tricks' (proxy, SECOND-HAND): ArchdukeTim and SamCarlberg both emphasize 'PIDF control cannot compensate for slop and backlash', and that proper tuning requires tensioned belts/chains and shimmed gears first. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pid-tuning-tips-tricks/502784 . Same thread: thatboyryba reports 'one rotation motor seems to need an entirely different P value' on a swerve — a hardware asymmetry masquerading as a tuning problem. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/tuning-ctre-swerve/497995 (proxy)
painPoints.libraryFix: Ship a `MechanicalHealthCheck` command that runs BEFORE tuning: drive small ± voltage steps and measure the deadband width (backlash), compare breakaway voltage in both directions (asymmetric friction), compare motor-encoder position against an absolute encoder (slip), and compare gains/currents across nominally identical modules. Fail loudly with a WPILib Alert naming the mechanical fault. Telling a student 'your belt is loose, fix that before touching kP' is worth more than any gain the library could compute, and no existing FRC library does this.

painPoints.problem: NT-based tuning is a competition liability and most implementations do not gate it
painPoints.evidence: DogLog is explicit: 'Tunable values are great for speeding up development at home, but at competitions it's best to avoid relying on NetworkTables for core robot functionality', and it ignores NT tunables under FMS by default. https://doglog.dev/reference/tunable-values . 6328's LoggedTunableNumber has NO FMS gate — it reads the dashboard unconditionally. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt/main/src/main/java/frc/robot/util/LoggedTunableNumber.java . CD thread 507361 (proxy, SECOND-HAND): teams report SmartDashboard causing loop-time overruns and moving to direct NT writes to avoid it. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/how-are-teams-implementing-adjustable-constants/507361 . FrcCatalyst's constant-time disabled path ('every TunableNumber.get() returns its cached default in constant time') shows the right shape. https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning
painPoints.libraryFix: Default-deny under FMS (DriverStation.isFMSAttached()), with an explicit opt-out. When disabled, `get()` must return a cached primitive with zero NT traffic and zero allocation. Rate-limit publishes and batch writes so the tuning layer costs ~nothing in the 20 ms loop; never write vendor configs over CAN unless a gain actually changed.

painPoints.problem: Deprecation churn will invalidate any library built naively against the 2026 API
painPoints.evidence: 2027 changelog: REMOVED Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver, RobotBuilder, RamseteController, RamseteCommand, Mecanum/SwerveControllerCommand, NetworkTables v3, and 'Remove LUTs from LTV controllers'; RENAMED motor `set()` → `setThrottle()` and 'Speeds' → 'Velocities' in signatures; swerve/differential kinematics made immutable; CoordinateSystem rejects left-handed systems; field origin/orientation changes; FPGA clock → monotonic clock; joystick POV becomes enums; Commands v3 + OpMode arrive alongside v2. 2026 already deprecated `Command.schedule()` in favor of `CommandScheduler.getInstance().schedule(Command...)`. Meanwhile ArmFeedforward's `calculate(pos, vel, accel)` and `calculate(angle, curVel, nextVel, dt)` are both @Deprecated(forRemoval=true, since='2025') in favor of `calculateWithVelocities`. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html , https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wpilibsuite/frc-docs/main/source/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.rst , https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/controller/ArmFeedforward.html
painPoints.libraryFix: Keep the tuning/identification core dependency-light: it needs only wpimath (feedforward classes, LinearSystemId, LinearQuadraticRegulator, Matrix, profiles) plus NT4 — all of which survive 2027. Isolate every volatile surface behind a thin adapter: command construction (v2 vs v3), motor output (`set` vs `setThrottle`), dashboard transport, and vendor gain sinks. Use `calculateWithVelocities` from day one. Do not build anything on Ramsete, SwerveControllerCommand, Shuffleboard, or SmartDashboard.

constraints: MUST publish tunables as plain NT4 doubles under `/Tuning/<Mechanism>/<gain>` — this is the only path that works in BOTH AdvantageScope tuning mode (which reads the `/Tuning` table) and Elastic (Text Display / Number Slider are the editable widgets). https://docs.advantagescope.org/overview/live-sources/tuning-mode/ , https://frc-elastic.gitbook.io/docs/additional-features-and-references/widgets-list-and-properties-reference.md

MUST NOT depend on AdvantageKit. 6328's LoggedTunableNumber requires `org.littletonrobotics.junction.networktables.LoggedNetworkNumber` and TunableControls requires AdvantageKit outright; small teams frequently do not run it. Provide an AdvantageKit-compatible surface without the dependency. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hammerheads5000/2026Rebuilt/main/src/main/java/frc/robot/util/LoggedTunableNumber.java , https://github.com/hammerheads5000/TunableControls

MUST NOT depend on Shuffleboard or SmartDashboard — both are REMOVED in 2027, along with PathWeaver, RobotBuilder, RamseteController/RamseteCommand, Mecanum/SwerveControllerCommand, NetworkTables v3, and the LUTs inside LTV controllers. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

MUST use `ArmFeedforward.calculateWithVelocities(pos, currentVel, nextVel)` (and the equivalent on Elevator/SimpleMotor). Both accel-taking and dt-taking `calculate()` overloads are @Deprecated(forRemoval=true, since="2025"). https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/controller/ArmFeedforward.html

MUST gate NT-driven tuning when `DriverStation.isFMSAttached()`, with disabled reads costing zero NT traffic and zero allocation (DogLog does this by default via DogLogOptions.ntTunables; FrcCatalyst returns cached defaults in constant time; 6328's does NOT gate). https://doglog.dev/reference/tunable-values , https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning

MUST define all gains in one canonical unit system (volts per SI unit, per wpimath: kS=V, kV=V·s/unit, kA=V·s²/unit, kG=V) and convert at the vendor boundary. Phoenix 6 gains are output-per-rotation where 'output' depends on the request type (voltage/duty cycle/TorqueCurrentFOC); REVLib uses rotations and RPM (kV in V/RPM, kA in V/(RPM/s)) and has its own kG/kCos/kCosRatio split. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/stable/docs/api-reference/device-specific/talonfx/basic-pid-control.html , https://docs.revrobotics.com/revlib/spark/closed-loop/units

MUST enforce safety interlocks structurally before any tuning routine actuates: soft limits configured, commanded-voltage ceiling, held-enable (whileTrue) so release aborts, auto-abort on limit approach / current spike / overspeed, and coast-mode required for bang-bang. WPILib is explicit that SysIdRoutine 'only creates voltage commands ... it is up to you to set up hard or soft limits to prevent injury or damage', and YAMS warns 'Live Tuning can be DANGEROUS please test in sim before the real' robot. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/system-identification/running-routine.html , https://yagsl.gitbook.io/yams/documentation/understanding/integrations.md , https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/bang-bang.html

MUST fit within the 20 ms loop on a roboRIO 2 (and later SystemCore): use streaming normal equations (XᵀX is 3×3 or 4×4, XᵀY is 3×1 or 4×1) rather than storing sample arrays, and solve once at the end. wpimath ships `Matrix.solveFullPivHouseholderQr` ('Solves the least-squares problem Ax=B using a QR decomposition with full pivoting') and bundles EJML. Teams already report SmartDashboard-driven loop overruns. https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/Matrix.html , https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/how-are-teams-implementing-adjustable-constants/507361 (proxy)

MUST NOT write vendor configs over CAN every periodic. FrcCatalyst calls `tunableGains.checkAndApply(motor)` on every periodic; gate on actual per-gain change and rate-limit, or a full tuning tab becomes a CAN-bus flood. https://tomas-1226.github.io/FrcCatalyst/advanced/tuning

SHOULD survive the Commands v2 → v3 transition: 2027 adds a Commands v3 Java framework plus an FTC-style OpMode framework and a declarative state-machine API on v3, while v2 persists. Expose behavior as plain objects/Runnables with thin command adapters rather than deep Command subclasses. Note `Command.schedule()` is already deprecated in 2026 in favor of `CommandScheduler.getInstance().schedule(Command...)`. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

SHOULD avoid encoding field-frame assumptions in anything tuning-related: 2027 changes the field coordinate system origin and orientation, makes swerve/differential kinematics immutable, renames 'Speeds' to 'Velocities' in signatures, renames motor `set()` to `setThrottle()`, and adds forward/inverse kinematics for ACCELERATIONS to the kinematics interface. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/2027/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

SHOULD NOT ship relay (Åström–Hägglund) or Ziegler–Nichols autotuning as the headline feature. Both deliberately drive the loop into sustained oscillation, which is unsafe on a geared FRC arm/elevator; the FRC-specific discussion holds that hand tuning is 'usually rated as superior to the autotune relay method' and that auto-tune 'is not for the uninitiated'. Prefer guided/assisted tuning (OLS + LQR + narrated recipe) that teaches rather than hides. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/automatic-pid-tuning/426844 (proxy)

SHOULD support sim-first tuning as the default promotion path — separate sim and real gains in config (YAMS does this with withSimClosedLoopController / withSimFeedforward) so students can run the whole recipe against WPILib's FlywheelSim/ElevatorSim/SingleJointedArmSim before arming hardware. https://yagsl.gitbook.io/yams/api-reference/java-reference/motor-controllers/motor-controllers/smart-motor-controller-config.md , https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/wpilib-tools/robot-simulation/physics-sim.html

SHOULD keep SysId interoperability as an escape hatch: emit WPILog-compatible output with a single routine per file and a string 'state' entry, since AdvantageKit logs are NOT directly SysId-loadable and require AdvantageScope re-export. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/system-identification/loading-data.html , https://docs.advantagekit.org/data-flow/sysid-compatibility/

(2) I could NOT read sysid's FeedbackAnalysis.cpp — the raw GitHub paths I tried 404'd — so the exact Q/R matrices SysId uses internally are INFERRED from WPILib's prose ('via LQR') plus the public wpimath API, not read from source. (3) FrcCatalyst claims (TunableGains, TunerLive, mechanism list) come solely from the project's own docs site; I did not read its source and cannot vouch for maturity or adoption. (4) YAMS adoption ('400+ teams') is the project's own claim. (5) I found no primary source giving a canonical FRC tuning recipe specifically for climbers or intake rollers — these are typically run open-loop with current limits rather than tuned, but I could not verify that from a primary source and it should be treated as unconfirmed.
